newsitem.title: DUBAI: $70 bln to be spent on Saudi contracting in 5 yrs.
newsitem.headline: $70 bln to be spent on Saudi contracting in 5 yrs.

text.p: Some 261 billion riyals ($70 billion) will be spent on construction projects and infrastructure maintenance in Saudi Arabia in the five years to 2000, according to a private study of the contracting industry.

Sixty percent will come from the public sector, including state oil-firm Saudi Aramco and petrochemicals giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp, said Anzar Ahmad, vice president of the Consulting Center for Finance and Investment, which carried out the study for the Riyadh Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Some 148 billion riyals will probably be spent on new projects with the rest channeled to existing work and on infrastructure maintenance, he told Reuters on Sunday by telephone from Riyadh.

Fewer new state-funded schemes will mean the market will look for direction from the private sector -- which is forecast to initiate two-thirds of all new projects, while 90 percent of operating and maintenance work will come from the government.

"The market will continue to be tight and new opportunities from the government will be limited. The private sector will be the driving force behind construction opportunities and by far the biggest area for construction will be housing," Ahmad said.

Thanks to a population growth rate of three to four percent, demand for homes in the oil-rich kingdom is expanding fast but state financing through its Real Estate Development Fund is set to slow in the years to 2000, Ahmad said.
This should prompt contractors to come up with innovative home financing tools for customers.

"For the sector to become stronger, the coming years must see the development of closer links between the contractor and the provider of financing. There may even be room for a specialised financial institution for this purpose," Ahmad said.

"Previously, the government was financing everything on a lump-sum basis...but with increasing constraints on government financing very often the successful contractor will be one who can bring in the financing to the project," Ahmad said.
Apart from housing, tourism would provide big development opportunities. Projects for religious pilgrims to Mecca and Medina would also be the basis of much contractor business.
Ahmad said about 10 billion riyals was earmarked for large development projects until 2000 in the two cities -- the sites of some of Islam's holiest shrines.
Another 10 billion is expected to be invested in developing tourism facilities in the kingdom, he added.
